title: Did medieval people think the Earth was flat?
hook: Columbus didn’t have to prove the Earth was round: scholars had taught it for centuries.
summary: No: medieval scholars taught that the Earth is a sphere; the flat-Earth story about them was invented in the 19th century.
cardText: No. Medieval monks and teachers taught that the Earth is a sphere. The story that they believed in a flat Earth came much later, in the 19th century.

cardBlocks.text: Picture Columbus facing frightened scholars who were sure his ships would sail off the edge of the world. It’s a famous scene, and it never happened. Around AD 700, the English monk Bede was already describing the Earth as a ball, not a disc. In the 13th century, Sacrobosco’s Treatise on the Sphere became the most popular astronomy textbook in universities, and it argued that the Earth is round.

Columbus’s critics weren’t arguing about the planet’s shape: they were worried about the distance and the trip back. The flat-Earth version only took hold in the 19th century, helped by writers such as Washington Irving, whose Columbus biography came out in 1828.
Medieval scholars knew the Earth was round; the myth that they didn’t was created in the 19th century.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In The Reckoning of Time, Bede called the Earth an orb and wrote that it is more like a ball than a shield or a wheel. He also used that shape to explain why the length of daylight changes with the seasons.

About five centuries later, Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at the University of Paris, wrote the Treatise on the Sphere. It circulated in manuscript for some 240 years and was printed again and again from 1476 into the early 1600s. For the Earth’s circumference, Sacrobosco used the figure worked out by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes, which is close to the modern value.

Columbus set out believing the Earth was much smaller than it is. The advisers at the Spanish court who doubted his plan were concerned about the distance and the return journey. Ironically, they used the Earth’s roundness itself as an argument against the voyage.

In Irving’s biography, Columbus faces theologians who, according to Irving, thought the Earth was flat like a plate; historians regard the scene as pure fiction. Later, John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White held up the supposed medieval flat Earth as proof of an endless war between science and religion, a thesis historians of science now reject.
A few writers, such as Lactantius and Cosmas, really did argue for a flat Earth. But they were rare, and 19th-century authors greatly exaggerated their influence.

claims.text: The English monk Bede, who lived around AD 700, described the Earth as a ball rather than a disc.

support.excerpt: In The Reckoning of Time, Bede (who lived circa CE 673-735) refers to the Earth as an “orb” and says that “it is not merely circular like a shield or spread out like a wheel, but resembles more a ball.”
already with the monk Bede (673-735) in the North of England we find a robust defense of the sphericity of the earth.

claims.text: Sacrobosco’s Treatise on the Sphere first circulated around 1230 and became the most popular university astronomy text.

support.excerpt: First circulated about 1230 C.E., Sacrobosco’s Sphere became the single most popular university text on astronomy, circulating in manuscript for 240 years, and then being printed again and again from 1476 all the way up to the beginning of the 17th century.

claims.text: Sacrobosco argued at length that the Earth is a sphere.

support.excerpt: since Sacrobosco argued every which way from Sunday that the Earth is a sphere

claims.text: In the debates at the Spanish court, Columbus’s critics worried about the distance and the difficulty of returning; they were not flat-earthers.

support.excerpt: In the debates at the Spanish court leading to his famous first Atlantic crossing, he was not opposed by fanatic, flat-earther clerics. They were instead concerned by the distance, the difficulty of return, and speculations regarding the antipodeans, etc.

claims.text: The idea that medieval people believed in a flat Earth arose in the 19th century; Washington Irving, whose Columbus biography appeared in 1828, was one of the first to promote it.

support.excerpt: No one before the 1830s believed that medieval people thought that the earth was flat.
His misrepresentations of the history of early New York City and of the life of Washington were topped by his history of Christopher Columbus (1828).

American writer and historian Washington Irving was one of the first to promote this myth. He wrote A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus in 1828—a book which freely mixed fact and fiction

claims.text: Irving’s biography showed Columbus facing theologians who, he claimed, believed the Earth was flat; historians regard the scene as fiction.

support.excerpt: It was he who invented the indelible picture of the young Columbus, a "simple mariner," appearing before a dark crowd of benighted inquisitors and hooded theologians at a council of Salamanca, all of whom believed, according to Irving, that the earth was flat like a plate.

claims.text: John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White used the supposed medieval flat-Earth belief as proof of a war between science and religion, a thesis historians of science reject.

support.excerpt: Historians of science, particularly those specialising in the history of science and religion, have refuted the ‘conflict thesis’, demonstrating it to be an invention of the late 19th century, cooked up amidst the heated debates over Darwin and the increasing secularization of science. John W. Draper and Andrew D. White are often implicated in this artificial construction of warfare between science and faith, and a grand proof of this conflict is the supposed medieval belief in a flat earth.
This vast web of falsehood was invented and propagated by the influential historian John Draper (1811-1882) and many prestigious followers, such as Andrew Dickson White (1832-1918)

claims.text: A few writers, such as Lactantius and Cosmas, did argue for a flat Earth, and their influence was exaggerated in the 19th century.

support.excerpt: They insisted that people like Cosmas (who wrote in CE 500s, at the very beginning of the Middle Ages) and Lactantius (who wrote around CE 250-375, well before the Middle Ages), who did argue for a flat Earth model were much more influential than they actually were.
